desc:
The string post is a valid postfix expression: single lowercase letters are operands and +, -, *, /, ^ are binary operators, each written after its two operands (for example ab+c*).

Write the expression in ordinary infix notation using as few round brackets as possible, such that reading the result back with the usual rules gives exactly the same operation tree. The usual rules: + and - have the lowest priority, * and / the middle one, ^ the highest. Equal priorities are applied from left to right, except ^ which is applied from right to left. The answer is unique.

Examples: ab+c* gives (a+b)*c; abc*+ gives a+b*c; abc-+ gives a+(b-c) (the brackets are needed, because a+b-c would be (a+b)-c); abc^^ gives a^b^c while ab^c^ gives (a^b)^c.
constraints: post contains only lowercase letters and the characters + - * / ^ and is a valid postfix expression
hints: Build the infix text bottom-up. When an operator is applied to two sub-expressions, you have to decide for each of them whether it needs brackets.
Keep a stack of pairs (text, priority of its outermost operator). A single letter counts as having a priority higher than every operator, so it never needs brackets.

A left operand needs brackets if its priority is lower than the operator's, or equal when the operator is ^ (right-associative). A right operand needs brackets if its priority is lower, or equal when the operator is not ^. Join the texts, and store the operator's priority with the result.
editorial: Process the postfix string with a stack of finished sub-expressions; each entry keeps its infix text and the priority of its top-level operator (letters get a priority above all operators). An operand is pushed as is. For an operator op pop the right operand b and the left operand a and decide where brackets are unavoidable.

A bracket is necessary exactly when removing it would change the parse. A child with a lower priority than op would be split by op, so it needs brackets on either side. A child with the same priority needs brackets when it sits on the side against which op groups: for left-associative operators the right operand (a-(b-c), a/(b*c)), for the right-associative ^ the left operand ((a^b)^c). A child with a higher priority never needs brackets. Because each bracket is added only when necessary, the count is minimal and the output is unique.
Push (a op b, priority(op)). At the end the stack holds the answer. Time O(n) for the stack work plus the cost of building strings (at most O(n) per concatenation, fine for n = 5,000).
